title: City Columns
description: Ten warm newspaper columns about everyday city life: a line at the bakery, a broken elevator, a rainy Monday, a neighbor's dog, a friendly bus driver, a power outage and the people who share a building and a street.

lessons.title: The Line at the Bakery
lessons.summary: A columnist explains why she waits in a long line outside a small bakery every Saturday morning.
lessons.text:
Every Saturday morning, at precisely 7 o'clock, a line begins to form outside the little bakery on Elm Street. By 7:30, it reaches the corner. By 8, it has turned the corner and continued past the flower shop. I know these times precisely, because for two years I have been standing in that line myself.

At first, I came only for the bread. Mr. Rossi, the baker, makes his bread with a starter, a living mix of flour and water that helps the bread rise. His grandmother brought the starter from Italy almost 70 years ago, and he still feeds it every night, as if it were a pet. He also bakes a dark bread full of seeds and fiber. My doctor keeps telling me to eat more fiber, so I buy a loaf every week and feel a little healthier just carrying it home.

Soon, however, I realized that the line itself was the real reason I came. Nobody in it is in a hurry. The people who are in a hurry go to the supermarket. The rest of us wait, talk and watch the street wake up.

There are the regulars. Two elderly sisters, who are identical twins, arrive in identical red coats and argue gently about the weather. A young father reads the newspaper while his daughter sleeps on his shoulder. And there is a small boy who comes with his grandma. While they wait, his grandma tells him the names of the trees on the street, and he repeats each one carefully, as though there might be a test later.

When they finally reach the counter, the boy always chooses the same snack: a soft roll with Swiss cheese inside. His grandma orders a sandwich with ham and Swiss cheese, and the two of them eat their snack on the bench outside, in the sun.

By the door, there is a shelf of yesterday's bread, sold for half price. It is the best bargain in the city. The twins always take the bargain bread, because, as one of them told me, they toast it anyway.

Last Saturday it rained, and I expected the line to be short. It was not. People stood under umbrellas and shared them with strangers. Nobody complained, and nobody left, except one man who was clearly in a hurry. He looked at his watch, then at the line, and hurried off.

I still come for the bread. But I stay for the line.

Questions:
When does the line begin to form?
It begins to form at precisely 7 o'clock every Saturday morning.
What is a starter?
A starter is a living mix of flour and water that helps the bread rise.
Why does the writer buy the dark bread?
She buys it because it is full of fiber, and her doctor tells her to eat more fiber.
What snack does the boy always choose?
He always chooses a soft roll with Swiss cheese inside.
Why is yesterday's bread a bargain?
It is a bargain because it is sold for half price.
What is the real reason the writer comes to the bakery?
The real reason is the line itself, where nobody is in a hurry and people talk and watch the street.

lessons.title: Nine Days Without the Elevator
lessons.summary: When the old elevator in a fifteen-floor building stops working, the neighbors meet each other on the stairs.
lessons.text:
Our building has fifteen floors and exactly one elevator. I live on the eighth floor, which means that I am always in the middle of the morning traffic.

The elevator is old. Its cabin is small, with wooden walls, a mirror and room for 6 people, or 4 people and a bicycle. Every morning, the cabin fills with people and empties again, floor by floor. We say good morning, look at the numbers above the door and wait for our floor. In ten years, I had never spoken more than a sentence to most of the people who lived above and below me.

Then, one Monday in March, a paper sign appeared in the lobby: "The elevator is not operational. We are sorry for the inconvenience." Nobody knew how long it would stay that way, so the first day was full of confusion. People pressed the button repeatedly, as if the elevator could be persuaded. Others read the sign repeatedly, as if it might change. The confusion ended only when the building manager explained that a part had to come from another state and that we would have to wait about a week.

So we endured the stairs. For a man on the eighth floor, it was not so bad. For Mr. Okafor, who lives on the fifteenth floor, it was much harder. He told me that he could endure almost anything, but not carrying his shopping up fifteen floors twice a week. Soon, people on the lower floors began to carry his bags for part of the way.

I found that the climb was hard mentally more than physically. When I thought about all eight floors at once, my legs felt heavy. So I mentally divided the climb into small parts: the second floor, where a woman plays the piano; the fourth floor, where someone always cooks with garlic; the sixth floor, where a window looks over the park. Going down, I counted backward from 8 to 1, the way children count before a game.

Most of all, we talked. We stopped on the landings between floors to rest, and resting turned into conversation. I learned the names of the piano player and the garlic cook. Mr. Okafor invited three of us for tea.

After nine days, the elevator was operational again. The cabin fills and empties as before. But now, in that small wooden room, nobody looks at the numbers above the door. We are too busy talking.

Questions:
How many floors does the building have, and where does the writer live?
It has fifteen floors, and the writer lives on the eighth floor.
What did the sign in the lobby say?
It said that the elevator was not operational.
Why was the first day full of confusion?
Nobody knew how long the elevator would stay broken.
How did other people in the building help Mr. Okafor?
They carried his bags for part of the way up to the fifteenth floor.
How did the writer make the climb easier?
He mentally divided it into small parts, and going down he counted backward from 8 to 1.
What changed after the elevator was operational again?
Now the people in the building talk in the cabin instead of looking at the numbers above the door.

lessons.title: A Rainy Monday
lessons.summary: On a rainy Monday, a columnist leaves her warm couch and discovers that the city in the rain is quieter and kinder.
lessons.text:
It rained overnight, and it was still raining when I woke up on Monday. I could hear it on the window before I opened my eyes: not a gentle sound, but a steady, heavy one, like a crowd of people tapping their fingers on a table.

The radio was already talking about it. The weather service had issued an advisory for the whole city: heavy rain until evening, strong wind, and a risk of water on the roads. The advisory asked people to stay home if they could. I could not. I had an important meeting at 10.

For a long moment, I sat on the couch in my coat and looked at the window. The couch has never felt so soft. It takes a special kind of courage to leave a warm couch on a wet Monday morning, and I am not sure I have it. But at last, I opened the door.

Our street is built on a slope. On dry days, I barely notice the slope, but that morning the water ran down it like a small river, carrying leaves and a single red glove. At the bottom of the slope, where the street meets the park, the path had turned into mud. A mother was pulling a little boy away from the mud, and the little boy, who was wearing yellow boots, was pulling just as hard toward it.

The wind threw cold drops against my cheek. A woman at the bus stop held her scarf over her cheeks and laughed when her umbrella turned inside out. Strangers smiled at each other in a way they never do when the sun is shining. The rain, I thought, makes us all members of the same club.

At work, half of my colleagues had stayed home, and the meeting was short. In the afternoon, my nephew sent me a message. He was home from school and terribly bored. I told him that people who are bored should look out the window, and he answered that the window was the most boring thing of all.

By 5 o'clock, the heavy rain had become a gentle one, soft and almost warm. On my way home, the clouds lifted, and I could see the ridge of green hills to the north of the city, which had been hidden all day. The ridge looked freshly washed. I stopped on the bridge to look at it, and so did several other people. None of us were in a hurry.

Questions:
When did the rain begin?
It began overnight, before the writer woke up.
What did the weather advisory ask people to do?
It asked people to stay home if they could.
What did the writer see at the bottom of the slope?
She saw that the path in the park had turned into mud, and a little boy was trying to reach it.
Why did the writer's nephew send her a message?
He was home from school and very bored.
What could the writer see when the clouds lifted?
She could see the ridge of green hills to the north of the city.

lessons.title: Biscuit, the Loyal Neighbor
lessons.summary: A columnist writes about the small dog next door, his owner, and the evening the dog went missing for an hour.
lessons.text:
My neighbor, Mrs. Lane, is a widow. Her husband died six years ago, and since then she has lived with Biscuit, a small gray dog with a white beard. The beard makes Biscuit look like an old professor who is about to give a lecture. He is very serious about his beard and does not like it when children touch it.

Biscuit is the most loyal creature I know. Every afternoon at 4, he sits by the window and waits for Mrs. Lane to come home from the library, where she volunteers. He does not move until he sees her hat at the corner. Even when it rains, the loyal little dog stays at his window. People talk about the loyalty of dogs as if it were something from old stories, but in our building, loyalty has a gray beard and sits by the window.

Mrs. Lane is a tender person, and she is tender with him in a way that is lovely to watch. She talks to him all day long. She asks his opinion about the weather and about her soup. She never yells at him, even when he barks at the mail carrier. "If you yell at a dog," she told me once, "he only learns that you are loud."

Biscuit, however, is easy to offend. If you walk past him without saying hello, he turns his back and refuses to look at you. I offended him once by forgetting his name, and it took two days and a piece of cheese before he forgave me.

His favorite possession is a toy rabbit. The rabbit was white once; now it is the color of old tea. He carries the rabbit everywhere and sleeps with it under his chin.

Last winter, one evening, Biscuit disappeared. Mrs. Lane knocked on my door, very pale. She had opened her door to take out the trash, and he must have sneaked out behind her. We looked on every floor and asked every neighbor. Nobody had seen him.

Then I remembered the basement. The laundry room is in the basement, and the machines there make the air warm. We went down the stairs, and there he was: asleep on a pile of clean towels, with the rabbit under his chin. He had sneaked down to the warmest room in the building.

Mrs. Lane picked him up and held him against her face. Biscuit, for once, did not complain about his beard.

Questions:
Who is Mrs. Lane?
She is the writer's neighbor, a widow who lives with her dog, Biscuit.
Why does Biscuit look like an old professor?
He looks like an old professor because he has a white beard.
How does Biscuit show his loyalty?
He waits by the window every afternoon until Mrs. Lane comes home.
Why does Mrs. Lane never yell at Biscuit?
She thinks that a dog who is yelled at only learns that you are loud.
How did Biscuit get out of the apartment?
He sneaked out behind Mrs. Lane when she opened her door.
Where did they find Biscuit?
They found him asleep on clean towels in the warm basement, with his toy rabbit.

lessons.title: The Driver of Route 12
lessons.summary: A bus driver who greets every passenger slowly changes the mood of a whole bus.
lessons.text:
Mr. Bell drives the number 12 bus from the river to the university. He is a tall, distinguished man with silver hair and a neat gray mustache, and he resembles a famous conductor more than a bus driver. Even in his blue uniform, he looks distinguished. Some passengers say that he resembles a judge from an old movie.

What makes Mr. Bell special, however, is not his appearance. It is the way he says good morning. He says it to every person who gets on, and he puts the emphasis on the first word: "Good morning." With that emphasis, it does not sound like a habit. It sounds like a fact he would like you to know.

According to the last census, about 600,000 people live in our city. Mr. Bell, it seems, is running a census of his own, one good morning at a time. If the people who run the census ever lose their numbers, they could simply ask him.

Legally, of course, he does not have to do any of this. Legally, a bus driver has to drive safely, stop at every stop and check that everyone has paid. Nobody requires him to smile. But Mr. Bell believes that his job is not solely to move people from one place to another. "If it were solely about moving people," he told me, "they could use a machine."

The same passengers occupy the same seats every morning. An old man with a newspaper occupies the seat by the back door. A blonde student, her hair in a long braid, occupies the seat right behind the driver, and she and Mr. Bell discuss her exams. When she passed her last exam, the blonde student brought him a coffee, and he talked about it all week.

Not everyone was charmed at first. When Mr. Bell began driving the route, a young man in a gray suit dismissed his greeting with a short nod and never looked up from his phone. Mr. Bell was not offended. He simply kept saying good morning. Last month, I heard the young man say it first.

This year, the city replaced the old buses on Route 12 with electric ones. They are quieter and create much less pollution, which is good news for a city where pollution is a serious problem in summer. Mr. Bell likes the new bus. "It's quiet," he says, "so now everyone can hear me."

Questions:
Who does Mr. Bell resemble?
He resembles a famous conductor more than a bus driver.
Where does Mr. Bell put the emphasis when he says good morning?
He puts the emphasis on the first word, "good."
What does a bus driver legally have to do?
He has to drive safely, stop at every stop and check that everyone has paid.
Who occupies the seat right behind the driver?
A blonde student with a long braid occupies that seat.
How did the young man in the gray suit react at first?
He dismissed the greeting with a short nod and looked at his phone.
Why are the new buses good for the city?
They are quieter and create much less pollution.

lessons.title: The Night the Lights Went Out
lessons.summary: During a summer power outage, the neighbors of a building meet in the yard and share a dinner from their warm refrigerators.
lessons.text:
At 6 o'clock on the hottest evening of July, every light in our building went out at once. The fans stopped, and the kitchens went silent. And, to the horror of every teenager in the building, the wireless internet disappeared.

For the first hour, everyone stayed inside and waited. I sat by the open window and listened to the voices from the other windows. "Is your wireless working?" someone called across the yard. "Nothing is working," someone answered.

By 7 o'clock, I began to worry about my food. I opened the refrigerator quickly and did an inventory: 4 eggs, half a chicken, some tomatoes, a few peppers and, at the top, a large box of ice cream that was already growing soft. It was not an impressive inventory, but I could not let it go to waste. The loss of the ice cream, I decided, would be a small tragedy.

I was not the only one who had made this decision. When I went down to the yard, I found that the other residents had begun to assemble there, each with a plate or a bag. Mr. Diaz from the third floor carried out his old gas grill, which he normally uses only on holidays. Within half an hour, about 30 people had assembled around it.

What followed was the best dinner I have had in years. Mr. Diaz began to roast everything people brought him: chicken, peppers, corn and even a few bananas. He always roasts food very slowly, he explained, so that it tastes of smoke. The family from the fifth floor made an enormous salad from everyone's vegetables. My tomatoes went into the salad, and my half chicken went onto the grill.

Everyone was generous. The couple who own the corner coffee shop brought cold drinks. Even the teenagers, who had looked so unhappy an hour before, were generous with the lights on their phones, so that we could see our food. My ice cream was saved from tragedy: the children finished it in ten minutes.

When it grew dark, someone lit candles on the tables. A girl from the first floor brought out a puzzle with a thousand pieces, and a group of adults and children began to put it together by the light of the candles. Nobody finished the puzzle, but nobody seemed to mind.

The power came back at midnight. The lights came on, the fans began to turn, and the wireless returned. And yet, for almost an hour, most of us stayed in the yard, beside the grill and the half-finished puzzle.

Questions:
What happened at 6 o'clock?
Every light in the building went out, and the wireless internet disappeared.
What did the writer find when she did an inventory of her food?
She found eggs, half a chicken, tomatoes, peppers and a box of ice cream.
Where did the residents assemble?
They assembled in the yard, around Mr. Diaz's gas grill.
How does Mr. Diaz roast his food?
He roasts it very slowly, so that it tastes of smoke.
What happened to the writer's tomatoes?
They went into the big salad that the family from the fifth floor made.
What did the girl from the first floor bring out?
She brought out a puzzle with a thousand pieces.

lessons.title: The Corner Grocery
lessons.summary: A columnist describes a week in the life of the small grocery on her corner and the woman who runs it.
lessons.text:
On the corner of my street, between a dry cleaner and a shoe repair shop, there is a small grocery called Haddad's. It has three narrow aisles, a wooden floor that sings when you walk on it, and a bell over the door. Mrs. Haddad has run the grocery for 22 years, and in that time she has learned the names of most of her customers and the favorite foods of all of them.

Her week begins early on Tuesday. At 5 in the morning, a big rig arrives from a warehouse across the river. The rig is far too long for our narrow street, so the driver parks it on the main road, and Mrs. Haddad and her son carry the cargo to the shop by hand. The cargo is always the same: boxes of fruit and vegetables, bags of flour, cans of tomatoes and fresh milk. By 7, the rig has gone back to the warehouse, and the shelves are full.

Mrs. Haddad buys rice, beans and nuts in bulk, in huge bags, and her customers bring their own jars to fill. Buying in bulk keeps the prices low, she says, and it means less plastic in the trash.

Plastic is a big topic on our street this year. A new city rule mandates that shops stop giving out plastic bags. Some shop owners complained about the mandate, but Mrs. Haddad simply sewed bags out of old fabric: curtains, old shirts and summer dresses from her own closet. Now customers choose their bag by its fabric. I carry my vegetables home in a bag of blue fabric that used to be her kitchen curtain.

At the back of the grocery, there is a small meat counter. Every Friday, Mr. Novak, who is 88, buys a pound of chicken liver. He cooks the liver with onions, the way his mother did, and he tells Mrs. Haddad every Friday that it is the best thing in the world.

On Saturday evening, Mrs. Haddad puts aside the bread and fruit she has not sold. She does not throw them away. Instead, she donates them to the shelter on Fourth Street. Last year, she says, she donated more than 2000 pounds of food.

Once a year, her nephew, who is an accountant, comes to audit the shop's books. The audit takes an entire Sunday. He always finds that the grocery earns very little money. And every year, Mrs. Haddad tells him that the audit is wrong, because it does not count the most important things.

Questions:
How long has Mrs. Haddad run the grocery?
She has run it for 22 years.
Why does the driver park the rig on the main road?
He parks it there because the rig is too long for the narrow street.
Why does Mrs. Haddad buy rice and beans in bulk?
Buying in bulk keeps the prices low and means less plastic in the trash.
What does the new city rule mandate?
It mandates that shops stop giving out plastic bags.
What does Mr. Novak buy every Friday?
He buys a pound of chicken liver, which he cooks with onions.
What does Mrs. Haddad do with the bread and fruit she has not sold?
She donates them to the shelter on Fourth Street.

lessons.title: Marathon Morning
lessons.summary: A columnist who cannot run watches the city marathon pass her street and helps at a water table.
lessons.text:
Once a year, in October, the city marathon passes down my street. For one morning, the cars disappear, the street fills with people, and the sound of running feet replaces the sound of traffic.

I have never run a marathon, and I never will. I have a chronic problem with my left knee, the kind of chronic pain that comes and goes with the weather. So, every year, I opt for the easier role: I stand on the sidewalk with a cup of coffee and cheer. This year, however, I opted to do something more useful. I volunteered at a water table near the 20-mile mark.

My neighbor Rachel, on the other hand, was running. She is 52, and she began running only four years ago, after a friend took her to a yoga class. The yoga, she says, taught her to breathe; the running taught her to keep going. She still does yoga twice a week, and she claims that yoga is the reason her knees are fine. I have tried yoga with my chronic knee, and I am not so sure.

The excitement started early. By 8 o'clock, families had brought chairs and signs. Children drew pictures on the road with colored chalk. When the first runners appeared at the top of the street, the excitement turned into a roar.

At the water table, my job was simple. I held out small paper cups, and the runners took them without stopping. Most of them could not swallow the water properly while running. They took one quick swallow and poured the rest over their heads. By noon, my shoes were completely wet.

Next to our table, a boy of about 8 asked his father whether a runner could take the subway for part of the race. "No," his father said, "that would be cheating." The boy thought about it for a moment. Then he asked if riding a bicycle would be cheating, too. "Also cheating," said his father.

The victor of the race, a young woman from Kenya, finished in just over 2 hours. We never saw her; by the time she passed our corner, the crowd was too thick. Rachel passed our table 3 hours later. She took a cup, swallowed half of it and waved to me without stopping.

She finished in 4 hours and 41 minutes. That evening, she showed me her medal. On our street, everyone who finished was a victor.

Questions:
Why has the writer never run a marathon?
She has a chronic problem with her left knee.
What did the writer opt to do this year?
She opted to volunteer at a water table near the 20-mile mark.
How did Rachel begin running?
She began after a friend took her to a yoga class.
Why did the runners pour water over their heads?
They could not swallow the water properly while running, so they took one swallow and poured the rest over their heads.
What did the boy's father say about taking the subway?
He said that it would be cheating.
Who was the victor of the race?
A young woman from Kenya was the victor; she finished in just over 2 hours.

lessons.title: The Artist on the Third Floor
lessons.summary: A neighbor who writes children's books draws the people of her building as animals, and they all wait for the book.
lessons.text:
For three years, I have lived across the hall from Ms. Ito, and for three years I have known her only as the woman with ink on her fingers. Last spring, I finally learned why. Ms. Ito writes and draws children's books. A small company in Boston publishes one of her books every year, and this year they plan to publish her tenth.

Her apartment is full of light. A large table stands by the window, covered with paper, brushes and jars of water in every color. Every illustration in her books begins on that table. She makes each illustration by hand, she told me, first in pencil and then in paint, and some of them take a whole week.

This spring, she was working against a deadline. The company wanted every picture by the first of June. When I visited her in May, there were drawings taped to every wall, and a calendar with the deadline circled in red. "I always think I have plenty of time," she said, "and then the deadline arrives like a train."

Ms. Ito knows how to render ordinary places beautifully. She renders the roofs of our neighborhood in soft blues and grays, so that they look like a calm sea. But it was her characters that made me laugh. Her new book is about a building full of animals, and she has decided to portray the people who live in her own building.

The woman on the first floor, who has a cloud of soft white hair, is portrayed as a sheep, knitting on her balcony. The old man on the fifth floor, who has a long white beard, has become a goat with reading glasses. The little dog from the second floor appears exactly as himself. And our building manager, who walks the halls every evening with his keys, is portrayed as the sheriff of the building: a serious brown bear with a silver star on his vest.

"Is the sheriff a good sheriff?" I asked her.

"The best," she said. "He fixes everything."

The hero of the story is a young rabbit with sandy fur, who is new in the building and does not know anyone. She is based on the girl from the sixth floor, whose family moved in last winter and who has sandy hair. In the book, the rabbit knocks on every door and makes a friend on every floor.

Ms. Ito met her deadline with two days to spare. The book will be published in the fall. Everyone in the building has already asked for a copy, especially the "sheep" and the "goat."

Questions:
What does Ms. Ito do?
She writes and draws children's books.
How does Ms. Ito make each illustration?
She makes it by hand, first in pencil and then in paint.
When was her deadline?
Her deadline was the first of June.
How does she portray the building manager?
She portrays him as the sheriff of the building, a brown bear with a silver star.
Who is the hero of the story?
The hero is a young rabbit with sandy fur who is new in the building.
Did Ms. Ito meet her deadline?
Yes, she met it with two days to spare.

lessons.title: Tuesday Afternoons with Mrs. Grant
lessons.summary: A retired teacher helps the children of her building with their homework, and one girl finally does well in mathematics.
lessons.text:
Mrs. Grant lives on the ground floor of our building, in the apartment with the red door and the window boxes full of herbs. For 35 years, she taught mathematics at the high school across the river. She retired five years ago, but she has not really stopped teaching.

Every Tuesday afternoon, from 4 to 6, the children of our building bring their homework to her kitchen. There are usually six or seven of them, between the ages of 9 and 15. Mrs. Grant does not charge anything. "I administered tests for 35 years," she says. "Now I would rather help children pass them than administer them."

Her greatest gift is patience. She explains the same problem three or four times, in three or four different ways, and never sounds tired. When I asked her how she kept her patience, she said that patience is not a feeling but a decision. "You decide it again every five minutes," she said.

Although she taught mathematics, she helps with everything. She corrects grammar in English essays, checks spelling and listens to children practice their speeches. She is strict about grammar. She once spent ten minutes explaining the difference between "fewer" and "less" to a boy who, I suspect, will remember it for the rest of his life.

There is one firm rule in her kitchen. All phones go into a basket by the door. "Phones distract you," she tells every new child. "And a distracted mind needs twice the time." Additionally, she does not allow television, music or talk about video games until the homework is finished. Additionally, there are always cookies, but only after the work.

The parents of the building can testify to the results. Grades have gone up on almost every floor. The father of the twins on the fourth floor once testified at a building meeting that his sons now actually enjoy fractions, a statement that seemed to surprise even him.

The best story belongs to Amira, who is 13 and lives on the seventh floor. Last fall, Amira was failing mathematics and had decided that she was "not a numbers person." Mrs. Grant did not agree. Every Tuesday, they worked through the problems slowly, one by one. In March, Amira took her big end-of-term test, and she aced it. She got 96 out of 100.

The next Tuesday, Amira came early. She brought a card that said, in careful handwriting, "Thank you for helping me ace it." Mrs. Grant put the card on her refrigerator, next to the cookies.

Questions:
What did Mrs. Grant teach for 35 years?
She taught mathematics at the high school across the river.
Why does Mrs. Grant say she would rather help children than administer tests?
She administered tests for 35 years, and now she would rather help children pass them.
What does Mrs. Grant say about patience?
She says that patience is not a feeling but a decision that you make again every five minutes.
Why do all phones go into a basket by the door?
They go into the basket because phones distract children from their homework.
What did Amira believe about herself last fall?
She believed that she was not a numbers person.
How did Amira do on her test in March?
She aced it and got 96 out of 100.
